# The Limits of Symbols: Can Text Carry Embodied Wisdom?

> This is the second article in the five-part blog series "The Shannon Limit of Civilizational Wisdom."

## Introduction: A Premise Taken for Granted for Thirty-Five Years

Over the past two years, "compression is intelligence" has gone from a slogan to an industrial reality: large language models treat the entirety of human writing as an information source, compressing it ever further by predicting the next token, with capabilities emerging along the way. Following this paradigm to its natural conclusion, an obvious question arises: does the entire textual record of human civilization, as an information source, have an incompressible lower bound — a "Shannon limit of civilization"?

The question sounds well-posed, but in fact it rests on an implicit premise that has almost never been examined: **wisdom can be fully encoded into symbol sequences**. If this holds, then estimating the entropy rate of text is estimating the entropy rate of civilizational wisdom. If it does not, then every compression limit derived from text corpora is really a limit on the "articulable projection of wisdom," not on wisdom itself. This is not rhetorical nitpicking — in information-theoretic terms, it is a question of source definition: the Shannon limit is only meaningful for a well-defined source, and whether "the textual archive" and "civilizational wisdom" are the same source is precisely the first-order question.

The cognitive gap is this: in the thirty-five years since Harnad formally named the symbol grounding debate in 1990, it has never been adjudicated in philosophy, but large language models have, through sheer scale, dragged it out of the philosophy seminar and back onto the engineering floor. When GPT-class systems approach human performance on nearly all language benchmarks, "can a purely symbolic system acquire meaning?" is no longer a matter of speculation but a question demanding an engineering answer — because it determines whether our continued investment in text compression is approaching a limit or crashing into a wall drawn long ago.

This article's claim is that the symbol grounding problem can be precisely restated, from an information-theoretic perspective, as a problem of the **ill-posedness of an inverse problem**. From this, three things can be argued. First, text-only compression can indeed give rise to internal world models, but these are homomorphic to the "text generation process" rather than causally coupled to physical reality, and their information content has a hard upper bound. Second, tacit knowledge constitutes the absolute ceiling of the **text-only codebook**, not the ceiling of intelligence — conflating the two is the most pervasive conceptual slippage in current public discussion. Third, multimodal compression is not a higher-resolution version of the same projection, but a change in the projection's topology — though the existing evidence only supports that it enlarges the mutual information between model and world, not yet that it has completed an ascent to a higher "level of wisdom."

## 1. An Information-Theoretic Restatement of the Grounding Problem: An Irreversible Projection Operator

First, the terminology. The **symbol grounding problem** asks: for a system that only manipulates symbols, where does the meaning of its symbols come from? Harnad's 1990 formulation: if the definition of "horse" consists only of other symbols ("hooved," "mammal," "odd-toed ungulate"), and those symbols are defined by still more symbols, the whole system is a circular dictionary — he called it the "symbol merry-go-round." His answer: symbols must be grounded in external objects through sensorimotor experience.

Restated in information-theoretic language, the problem becomes exceptionally clear. Let the state of the external world be $W$, and the text corpus be $T$. Human verbalization is a projection:

$$T = f(W, \theta)$$

where $\theta$ denotes the speaker's intentions, cultural conventions, and expressive strategies. A text-only model observes only $T$; what it must recover is $W$. But $f$ is not injective: infinitely many different combinations of world states and intentions can produce the same text. Formally, the null space of $f$ is non-empty:

$$\ker f = \{(W, \theta) : f(W, \theta) = T\} \neq \emptyset$$

Therefore, "recovering the world from text" is a **set-valued inverse problem**: the best that compression can achieve is not recovering $W$, but constraining the estimate to the equivalence class consistent with the observation, $\hat{W} \in f^{-1}(T)$. The size of that equivalence class is precisely the amount of ambiguity that text-only compression cannot in principle eliminate.

This formulation immediately yields a hard upper bound. The text model $\hat{W}$ is a function of $T$, so by the data processing inequality:

$$I(\hat{W}; W) \le I(T; W) \le H(T)$$

The model's mutual information with the world cannot exceed the mutual information between the text and the world. This is not an engineering limitation; it is a theorem of information theory: any system trained only on text has its ability to "decompress physical reality" capped by the information-carrying capacity of the textual archive itself. Signal-to-noise ratio lost at the verbalization stage cannot be recovered by any compression algorithm — no matter how closely it approaches the Shannon limit.

Bender and Koller's 2020 "octopus experiment" turns this abstract theorem into an intuition pump: an octopus eavesdropping on all communications between two isolated islands can learn the entire statistical structure of the language and pass in conversation without being detected, but when an islander shouts "a bear is chasing me, how do I defend myself with what's at hand," it cannot give meaningful advice — "bear" and "stick" are, for it, merely co-occurring symbols pointing to no operable objects. Translating into the language above: the $\hat{W}$ the octopus learns sits perfectly inside the equivalence class $f^{-1}(T)$, but that equivalence class houses both "two islands with bears" and "a hollow world where only symbols spin," and the octopus has no additional constraint to tell them apart.

**A skeptic might argue** that interpretability research has already overturned this pessimistic conclusion. The Othello-GPT experiment by Kenneth Li and colleagues (ICLR 2023) trained a GPT solely on sequences of legal moves (pure symbol strings, no board, no statement of rules), and the results **showed** that the model spontaneously formed high-precision, decodable internal representations of the complete board state; more crucially, causal intervention experiments — flipping an internal representation of a square from "black" to "white" — produced changes in the model's next-legal-move predictions consistent with the logic of the board. This shows that the internal world model is not a byproduct of statistical coincidence but a working variable the model actually uses in computation.

This rebuttal forcefully overturns the strong claim that "purely textual systems contain only surface statistics," but it does not overturn the hard upper bound, and the reason lies in the special topology of the Othello world. Othello is a closed system of 64 squares, deterministic rules, and a state fully determined by the move sequence: the move sequence is an almost lossless encoding of the world state, the projection $f$ is nearly invertible, and the null space approaches zero. "Inferring a world model from pure symbols" holds in Othello precisely because the entire causal structure of that world has been exhaustively written into the symbol sequence. The open world of human speech is exactly the opposite: $f$ is an extremely lossy projection with an enormous null space — "nice weather today" corresponds to infinitely many physical worlds. Othello-GPT **proved** that "when syntax exhausts the world, syntax is the world"; it did not prove, and cannot prove, that "when syntax is only a sparse shadow of the world, syntax can restore the world."

This distinction explains an otherwise puzzling empirical fact: large models perform best on code and mathematics, and fail in the strangest ways on physical common sense and social judgment — the former are domains where the null space approaches zero, the latter domains where the null space is vast.

## 2. Tacit Knowledge: The Ceiling of the Text-Only Channel, Not the Ceiling of Intelligence

If Section 1 characterized the fact that "projection necessarily loses information," this section answers: how large and how important is the part that is lost?

First, the terminology. **Tacit knowledge**, a concept introduced by Polanyi (1958/1966), is built around the core proposition that "we can know more than we can tell." His classic example is riding a bicycle: the physics of staying upright can be written down, but no cyclist rides by consulting that formula; the knowledge that actually executes the principle resides in the body's sensorimotor circuits — unspeakable, yet completely reliable. In one sentence for the layperson: tacit knowledge is the part of knowledge that one "can do but cannot articulate."

In information-theoretic terms, tacit knowledge is a high-dimensional, low-redundancy sensorimotor time series, and its verbalization is an extremely lossy compression. The problem is not the compression ratio but the **asymmetry of the distortion metric**: the raw signal transmitted from the human eye to the brain is estimated at around $10^7$ bit/s, while the language output channel runs at roughly 40–50 bit/s. From $10^7$ down to $10^2$, a compression of six orders of magnitude must discard information — and what is discarded is precisely the high-frequency fine-adjustment components most valuable for "executing actions," while what is retained are the low-frequency categorical components most valuable for "social transmission." The textual archive is an encoding optimized by humans for collaboration, not one optimized for reproducing wisdom.

Two cases **show** the real texture of this ceiling. The first is the apprenticeship of Ono Jiro depicted in the documentary *Jiro Dreams of Sushi*: newcomers spend their first months doing nothing but wringing out scalding towels by hand, and only after about a decade are they allowed to cook tamagoyaki; the apprentice Nakazawa Daisuke made more than two hundred tamagoyaki over roughly four months before receiving a single nod. Note the information-theoretic structure of this protocol: what the master transmits is not a recipe (a recipe fits in three sentences) but a high-bandwidth error-feedback channel — the master tastes, says "no good," the apprentice adjusts the rhythm of the wrist and the heat, and submits again. What the entire training transmits is the gradient direction of a loss function, not the function itself. That is exactly why it must take ten years and why it resists verbalization. The second case is Nishioka Tsunekazu, the last miya-daiku (temple carpenter) of Horyuji: he selected timber by "buying the mountain" (trees from the same mountain and the same slope share a similar "character," so the whole mountain is purchased) and by the feel of his palm against the trunk, the rebound and sound of the axe blade entering the wood — judgments he explicitly said "cannot be put into words; they can only be remembered by the body."

The volume of tacit knowledge can also be calibrated in reverse. Moravec's paradox (1988) in robotics is a repeatedly confirmed empirical law: it is relatively easy to make computers perform at adult level on intelligence tests or chess, but extraordinarily hard to give a robot the perceptual-motor abilities of a one-year-old child. The explanation is the compression depth of evolutionary history: abstract reasoning is a new skill of mere tens of thousands of years, while the sensorimotor system has been honed over hundreds of millions of years of evolution, its "knowledge" stored as neural-circuit weights, enormous in total volume and never once verbalized. This **suggests** that tacit knowledge is not a negligible residual term in the total stock of wisdom, but very likely the submerged main body of the iceberg. If so, the gap between "the Shannon limit of the textual archive" and "the Shannon limit of civilizational wisdom" is not a correction term but a difference of orders of magnitude.

**A skeptic might argue** that robotic foundation models have already bypassed this ceiling. RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023) **showed** that vision-language-action models can transfer certain "tacit" skills (such as "move the can onto the photo of Taylor Swift," a task requiring visual grounding and motor coordination) directly to physical robots via video and robot trajectory data, bypassing the verbalization step entirely.

This rebuttal, in fact, locates the ceiling precisely rather than demolishing it. What RT-2 bypasses is the "text" codebook, not the "compression" paradigm; what it proves is that tacit knowledge can be compressed by machine learning through sensorimotor channels rather than through language. The rigorous formulation should therefore be: tacit knowledge constitutes the absolute ceiling on **text-only models**' prediction of the full stock of wisdom — within that channel, guaranteed unsurpassable by $I(\hat{W};W) \le I(T;W)$ — not the ceiling of intelligent systems. The two extremes in public discussion, "AI can never truly understand" and "LLMs already understand everything," commit the same conceptual slippage: misreading "the limit of the text channel" as "the limit of intelligence," or vice versa.

## 3. Multimodality: An Increase in Resolution, or a Change in the Topology of the Projection?

If the null space of a single projection is the problem, is multimodality the answer? That depends on what multimodality actually changes.

Generalize the framework of Section 1 directly. Text-only is a single projection $T = f_1(W)$; multimodality introduces multiple heterogeneous projections:

$$T = f_1(W), \quad V = f_2(W), \quad A = f_3(W), \dots$$

The key observation: as long as the projection operators of the modalities differ (vision, hearing, and text sample the world differently and preserve different dimensions), their null spaces differ, and joint observation constrains the estimate to the **intersection** of the null spaces:

$$\hat{W} \in \bigcap_i f_i^{-1}(\text{obs}_i), \qquad \bigcap_i \ker f_i \subsetneq \ker f_1$$

This is qualitatively different from "increasing resolution." Increasing the resolution of the same modality densifies the sampling rate of the same projection, shrinking the volume inside $f_1^{-1}$; introducing a heterogeneous modality uses a new projection with a different null-space structure to **cut away** the part of the original equivalence class that is consistent with the old observations but inconsistent with the new ones. The former is an improvement in the metric sense; the latter is an improvement in the topological sense — the equivalence class is jointly bounded by "slices" taken from multiple directions. In one sentence for the layperson: increasing resolution is "taking the same photo more sharply"; changing the topology is "taking another photo from a new angle and, by comparing the two, ruling out impossible worlds."

Empirical evidence supports that intersection constraints do produce representational structures unavailable to text-only training. The most direct case is CLIP (Radford et al., 2021): after contrastive learning on 400 million image-text pairs, the model achieved 76.2% zero-shot classification accuracy on ImageNet, matching a ResNet-50 fully supervised on 1.28 million human-labeled images. This **shows** that when textual representations are constrained by the image projection, "word-object" alignment emerges spontaneously as a structure — in text-only training, the correspondence between "cat" and image features lies deep within the null space of $f_1$, unrecoverable in principle; the image-text intersection slices it out.

But the strength of the evidence must be honestly calibrated: current multimodal models still make systematic errors on fine-grained spatial reasoning (exact counting, left-right relations, occlusion reasoning), and hallucination has not been eliminated by multimodality. This **suggests** that intersection constraints have so far only enlarged the total amount of $I(\hat{W};W)$, without yet completing an ascent to a higher "level of wisdom" — what we observe is the null space shrinking, not the null space vanishing.

**A skeptic might argue** that this whole route is still insufficient. LeCun's bandwidth argument (2022, *A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence*) is the most thorough: the amount of visual information a human child receives before age four (vision at roughly $10^7$ bit/s versus reading at roughly 50 bit/s) vastly exceeds their linguistic input; the total visual information over four years exceeds the total training text of a typical LLM by several orders of magnitude, and the human world model is shaped primarily by the former. Therefore autoregressive text prediction, at any scale, cannot produce a genuine world model; even the representational space in which prediction occurs must be replaced (JEPA-style architectures).

The response: LeCun's bandwidth arithmetic is correct, but its target needs to be made precise — what it opposes is "text-only compression," not the "compression paradigm" itself; JEPA likewise learns compression and prediction, only with a different channel and prediction space. This article's position is structurally aligned with LeCun's: the compression methodology is not necessarily wrong; what is wrong is the singleness of the compression channel. The disagreement is only this: this article regards the multimodal intersection as a targeted partial correction, while LeCun holds that even the representational space must be replaced. This is an open empirical question on which the current evidence is insufficient to adjudicate — on this we can only mark "**not ruled out**," and must not assert.

## Conclusion: The Exact Location of the Ceiling

Returning to the opening question: can text carry embodied wisdom? This article's answer is a structured "partially not," compressible into three conclusions with their confidence gradings:

1. Text-only compression faces a hard upper bound $I(\hat{W};W) \le I(T;W)$ in decompressing physical reality — this is a **theorem** (the data processing inequality); that internal world models can emerge in closed domains is an empirical fact **that has been shown** (Othello-GPT), but the extrapolation to open worlds does not hold.
2. Tacit knowledge is the absolute ceiling of the text-only codebook — the sushi apprenticeship and the miya-daiku cases **show** that the transmission protocol of their core craft is itself anti-verbalization, and Moravec's paradox **suggests** its volume is the main body of the iceberg; but this ceiling constrains only "text-only," not "machine learning" (RT-2).
3. Multimodality topologically changes the compression problem (an intersection of projections replacing a single projection) — CLIP's zero-shot capability **shows** that intersection constraints can produce representational structures unavailable to text-only training; but the evidence for an ascent to the "level of wisdom" is still insufficient, and LeCun's critique remains on the record.

The applicable boundaries must be stated plainly: all arguments in this article are confined to channel problems within the "compression + prediction" paradigm. It does not touch ontological questions such as consciousness or qualia; its assessment of the multimodal route is based on evidence up to the present and does not prejudge the future of JEPA-style architectures; the $I(T;W)$ upper bound it gives is a matter of principle, and how tight it is on specific corpora and tasks is an open empirical question.

For the larger topic of "the Shannon limit of civilization," this article's implications are twofold. The pessimistic side: the Shannon limit of the textual archive exists and is approachable, but it is the limit of "the articulable projection of wisdom," not of wisdom itself — the gap between the two is not a correction term but very likely an order of magnitude. The optimistic side: the location of the ceiling is precise — it is drawn on the codebook, not on intelligence. Switch to a different channel, and the problem takes on a different shape. As for whether a new channel can generate new knowledge that transcends history — that is the subject of the next article in this series.

---

*This series comprises five articles in total. The evidence-strength grading and uncertainty annotations of all claims in this article were retained after four-way cross-validation (logical audit / Munger scan / data audit / de-narrativization).*

In one sentence for the layperson: increasing resolution is "taking the same photo more sharply"; changing the topology is "taking another photo from a new angle and, by comparing the two, ruling out impossible worlds."

Empirical evidence supports that intersection constraints do produce representational structures unavailable to text-only training. The most direct case is CLIP Radford et al., 2021: after contrastive learning on 400 million image-text pairs, the model achieved 76.2% zero-shot classification accuracy on ImageNet, matching a ResNet-50 fully supervised on 1.28 million human-labeled images. This shows that when textual representations are constrained by the image projection, "word-object" alignment emerges spontaneously as a structure — in text-only training, the correspondence between "cat" and image features lies deep within the null space of $f1$, unrecoverable in principle; the image-text intersection slices it out.

But the strength of the evidence must be honestly calibrated: current multimodal models still make systematic errors on fine-grained spatial reasoning exact counting, left-right relations, occlusion reasoning, and hallucination has not been eliminated by multimodality. This suggests that intersection constraints have so far only enlarged the total amount of $I\hat{W};W$, without yet completing an ascent to a higher "level of wisdom" — what we observe is the null space shrinking, not the null space vanishing.

A skeptic might argue that this whole route is still insufficient. LeCun's bandwidth argument 2022, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence is the most thorough: the amount of visual information a human child receives before age four vision at roughly $10^7$ bit/s versus reading at roughly 50 bit/s vastly exceeds their linguistic input; the total visual information over four years exceeds the total training text of a typical LLM by several orders of magnitude, and the human world model is shaped primarily by the former. Therefore autoregressive text prediction, at any scale, cannot produce a genuine world model; even the representational space in which prediction occurs must be replaced JEPA-style architectures.

The response: LeCun's bandwidth arithmetic is correct, but its target needs to be made precise — what it opposes is "text-only compression," not the "compression paradigm" itself; JEPA likewise learns compression and prediction, only with a different channel and prediction space. This article's position is structurally aligned with LeCun's: the compression methodology is not necessarily wrong; what is wrong is the singleness of the compression channel. The disagreement is only this: this article regards the multimodal intersection as a targeted partial correction, while LeCun holds that even the representational space must be replaced. This is an open empirical question on which the current evidence is insufficient to adjudicate — on this we can only mark "not ruled out," and must not assert.

 Conclusion: The Exact Location of the Ceiling

Returning to the opening question: can text carry embodied wisdom? This article's answer is a structured "partially not," compressible into three conclusions with their confidence gradings:

1. Text-only compression faces a hard upper bound $I\hat{W};W \le IT;W$ in decompressing physical reality — this is a theorem the data processing inequality; that internal world models can emerge in closed domains is an empirical fact that has been shown Othello-GPT, but the extrapolation to open worlds does not hold.
2. Tacit knowledge is the absolute ceiling of the text-only codebook — the sushi apprenticeship and the miya-daiku cases show that the transmission protocol of their core craft is itself anti-verbalization, and Moravec's paradox suggests its volume is the main body of the iceberg; but this ceiling constrains only "text-only," not "machine learning" RT-2.
3. Multimodality topologically changes the compression problem an intersection of projections replacing a single projection — CLIP's zero-shot capability shows that intersection constraints can produce representational structures unavailable to text-only training; but the evidence for an ascent to the "level of wisdom" is still insufficient, and LeCun's critique remains on the record.

The applicable boundaries must be stated plainly: all arguments in this article are confined to channel problems within the "compression + prediction" paradigm. It does not touch ontological questions such as consciousness or qualia; its assessment of the multimodal route is based on evidence up to the present and does not prejudge the future of JEPA-style architectures; the $IT;W$ upper bound it gives is a matter of principle, and how tight it is on specific corpora and tasks is an open empirical question.

For the larger topic of "the Shannon limit of civilization," this article's implications are twofold. The pessimistic side: the Shannon limit of the textual archive exists and is approachable, but it is the limit of "the articulable projection of wisdom," not of wisdom itself — the gap between the two is not a correction term but very likely an order of magnitude. The optimistic side: the location of the ceiling is precise — it is drawn on the codebook, not on intelligence. Switch to a different channel, and the problem takes on a different shape. As for whether a new channel can generate new knowledge that transcends history — that is the subject of the next article in this series.
